title: Careers pages for a team of ten
metaTitle: Careers pages for a team of ten
excerpt: Say how the work goes and which roles are open now. A culture page with no jobs is a poster. Candidates need the work, the role, and how to apply.
alt: A workshop where one person points at colorful sticky notes while others sit with laptops. The working table fits a piece about describing how a small team actually works.
caption: Show the work, and the role that is actually open. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a small company's careers page say?
faqs.answer: How the work actually goes, and what you are hiring for now. Describe the rhythm of a week, who decides what, and where the work happens. Then list open roles with a real description and a way to apply. If nothing is open, say so, and do not leave a culture manifesto pretending to be a job board.

faqs.question: Should you keep a careers page with no open roles?
faqs.answer: A short note is enough. 'No open roles right now' plus how you work, if people genuinely ask, is honest. A full culture page with values, perks, and a gallery, and no jobs, reads as a poster. Take the nav item down until you are hiring, or reduce it to a sentence on the about page.

faqs.question: What belongs in a role description?
faqs.answer: The work they will do in the first months, who they will work with, and what you will not expect them to be. Location or remote rules, compensation shape if you can say it, and the application path. A list of fifteen virtues is not a description. Candidates skim for the job itself.

markdown:
Say how the work actually goes, and say what you are hiring for now. That is a useful startup careers page for a team of about ten. A culture page with no open roles is a poster. Candidates arrive to see if there is a job and if the week is one they want. Give them those two facts before you give them a mood.

Google's people-first guidance asks who created a page and how, and whether a reader leaves able to act. A careers page is that kind of page. The "how" is the way the team works. The action is the application, or a clear statement that you are not hiring. Anything else is atmosphere.

## The open role is the page

Lead with the jobs. If there is one role, the page can be that role. Title, what they will do, what a strong first six months looks like, and how to apply. The company story can be a short block above or beside it. It should not be a long scroll the job is buried under.

Write the work in verbs a candidate can imagine on a Tuesday. "You will pair with a founder on the marketing site, write the headings, and ship in the same repository as the engineer." That is a week. "You will own the brand journey and evangelize excellence" is a poster. People who have had a job can tell the difference in a sentence.

Say what the role is not. Not a team of five reporting to you. Not a research department. Not unlimited scope. Small companies hire people who will do the work, then accidentally describe a vice president. The mismatch shows up in the interviews you both regret. Fix it in the description.

If two roles are open, give them equal structure so they can be compared, and do not make one of them a leftover paragraph. If a role is closed, take it down the day it closes. A ghost job wastes a candidate's evening and wastes your inbox. It also makes the real opening look less real.

## How the work goes

Describe the rhythm without the mythology. How decisions get made. How feedback lands. What "soon" means. Whether people are in one city, spread out, or mixed. A team of ten has a texture a candidate can understand if you write it plainly. They do not need a culture deck to picture ten people.

Name the tools only where they change the job. A design role that lives in Figma and reviews in the browser is a different job from one that hands off static screens and disappears. An engineering role in TypeScript, React, and Next.js is a fact a candidate uses to opt in. A list of every SaaS logo on the wall is not a description of the work. Mention the ones that shape the day.

Be honest about the mix of making and talking. Early teams often need someone who can talk to a customer and then do the work. Say that, if it is true. Do not advertise a quiet specialist role and then spend the interview explaining that everyone does support. Surprises belong in the posting, not in week two.

Perks are last, and only the ones you actually have. A stipend you pay, a real holiday policy, equipment you provide. A ping-pong table in a photo of an office you no longer rent is the kind of error a candidate can see. Google's notes on helpful content treat checkable mistakes as trust problems. A careers page is full of checkable claims. Keep them current.

## What a culture page without roles does

It attracts people you cannot hire, then forces you to send a kind rejection to every one of them, or worse, to ignore them. The ignore is how a small company gets a reputation in a community that talks. If you are not hiring, close the door politely. "We are not hiring. The work we do is described on the site." That is complete.

Values on their own are not a door. Every company says it cares about quality and kindness. A candidate cannot choose you from that. They can choose from a role, a piece of work, and a sentence about how critique happens. If you want to publish how you work, publish it as a note from the studio, in the journal, where it does not pretend to be an application.

Photos of the team need the same honesty. Current people, a real room or a real remote setup, permission from the faces. A stock workshop is the logo-wall mistake applied to your own employees. If the team does not want to be on the site, use the work as the portrait. The work is why a good candidate is interested.

Do not keep a "talent community" form if you will not write back. A form is a promise. The confirmation should say whether any human reads general applications. If the answer is no, do not collect the names. Wanting a pile of résumés for later is not a reason to imply a process.

## The facts a candidate needs

Location rules, in one paragraph. Remote, a city, a number of days together. Time zones you can overlap. Sponsorship if you know the answer, and a plain no if the answer is no. Dodging this wastes the first interview. Put it high enough that a skim catches it.

Compensation shape if you can say it. A range, or a statement that you discuss pay in the first conversation and here is how you think about it. Silence is a strategy. It is also why strong candidates skip the form. You do not have to publish a number you have not decided. You do have to avoid a posting that feels like a trap.

The application path should be short. A letter and a link to work, or a form with a few questions you will actually read. A portal that asks them to retype their résumé into twenty fields tells a maker you do not respect time. You are a team of ten. You can read an email. Say which address, and what to include so you can be fair.

Say when they will hear. A true window, even a slow one, beats a void. Then keep it. The confirmation page after they apply is part of the careers page. What you received, what happens next, when. Silence after a careful application is the culture, whether you meant it to be or not.

## Tone, and the company they are judging

Write like the person they will work with. A careers page that suddenly becomes a different brand voice, full of hype and nicknames, feels like a recruiting ad bolted on. Use the same type, the same header, and the same plain sentences as the rest of the site. The candidate is also a reader of the product. The seam is visible.

Skip the wartime metaphors and the family metaphors. Both overclaim. A job is a job. You can be warm about the work without borrowing the language of a crisis or a household. "We are a small team and the work is close to the customer" is plenty of identity.

Show a piece of the real work nearby. A link to a project, a product screen, a writing sample from the studio. Candidates who are any good will look. Make the looking easy. If the public site is vague, the careers page cannot compensate with adjectives. Fix the homepage if that is what a hire will judge. They will judge it.

The people who interview should recognize the posting. If the description promises mentorship you do not have, or a roadmap you have not written, the interview will contradict the site. Share the draft with the person who would manage the role. Their edits are the accuracy pass. A founder writing alone will describe the job they wish existed.

## Keeping it current

Review the page every time a role opens or closes, and on a quiet month even if nothing changed, so the "how we work" paragraph is still true. Teams of ten change shape fast. A paragraph about pairing that you no longer do is a small lie with a long tail.

Remove the nav link when it points at nothing. Add it back when there is a role. Navigation is not a place to manifest a recruiting function. The about page can hold a sentence in the meantime, with an email if you truly want exceptional notes. Read that email or do not print it.

When you hire, update the page that same week. The role comes down. The description of the team, if it names a headcount or a shape, changes if you mention those things. You do not need to announce the hire as press. You do need the door to match the building.

Hanabi's own site stays aimed at client work. A careers story for a different company should be just as specific as that work: a real role, a real week, a real way to write. That specificity is what a good person trusts.

If you are hiring and the public site does not yet sound like the team you are asking them to join, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the posting and the homepage. The gap between them is the brief.

Legal pages are the other place a small site often looks like a different company. [Legal pages that are still part of the brand](/blog/legal-pages-that-are-still-part-of-the-brand) is the next piece, on setting privacy and terms in your own type instead of a default in a new window.
